apple.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Las Vegas Valley winters bank enough chill for low and moderate chill apples; the University of Nevada, Reno field trial confirms the crop fruits dependably here when the variety is matched to the chill (see the variety guidance). Summer heat and sunburn on young bark, not frost, are the practical hazards; early bloom in March clears the late-February last frost in most years.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Apples fruit reliably in Las Vegas if you pick a low or moderate chill variety the local trial confirmed. Heat, not cold, is the thing to manage; shade young trunks their first summers.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in early March usually clears the late-February last frost; an unusually late cold snap during bloom is an occasional, not typical, risk. Heat and sunburn are the larger hazards here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank more chill (roughly 500 to 900 hours), clearing the moderate chill varieties comfortably and edging toward the lower end of the high-chill group; bloom runs a couple of weeks later than the valley floor, after the mid-March last frost.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The higher, cooler parts of the region get more winter chill, so a wider range of apples fruits well. Bloom comes a little later here, after the March frost.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in April clears the mid-March last frost in most years; a late frost at the higher elevations during bloom is the occasional risk to watch.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin and the warm Colorado River corner (zone 10) bank the least chill, roughly 150 to 450 hours, so only the lowest-chill varieties (Anna, Dorsett Golden, Ein Shemer) fruit dependably; the moderate and high-chill sorts are unreliable this warm. Heat and sunburn are the dominant hazards.
10.suitability_note_beginner: It is warmest at Laughlin, with the least winter chill, so stick to the lowest-chill apples like Anna and Dorsett Golden. Heat is the main challenge.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the problem at Laughlin; intense summer heat and sunburn on young bark are the real hazards, and low winter chill limits the variety list.

apple.region_notes_beginner: Apples grow well in the Las Vegas Valley if you choose the right variety. A University of Nevada field trial confirmed dependable performers like Dorsett Golden, Anna, Pink Lady, Fuji, Mutsu, and Granny Smith; the highest-chill types like Honeycrisp and McIntosh need more winter cold than the desert reliably gives. Plant a bare-root or container tree while it is dormant, from late fall through winter, and shade young trunks against the summer sun.
apple.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) fruits apple dependably when the variety is matched to the region's chill, per a University of Nevada, Reno Extension field trial at the North Las Vegas Research Orchard. Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours; the trial's confirmed performers (Dorsett Golden, Pink Lady, and Mutsu as top choices, plus Anna, Fuji, and Granny Smith) span the low to moderate chill range, while the high-chill quarter of the standard variety list is unproven here. Bloom runs early, from late February at Laughlin through April in the cooler zone 8 pockets, and fruit ripens across summer. Heat and sunburn on young bark, not frost, are the main constraints. Plant bare-root or container trees during the dormant season.
apple.chill_basis_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours in zone 9, more in the cooler, higher zone 8 pockets and less at Laughlin in zone 10, enough to fruit a real range of low and moderate chill apples but not the highest-chill sorts. A University of Nevada, Reno Extension field trial at the North Las Vegas Research Orchard (2005 to 2018) confirms the dependable performers here: Dorsett Golden, Anna, Pink Lady, Mutsu, Fuji, and Granny Smith all fruit, with Dorsett Golden, Pink Lady, and Mutsu rated top choices, and the low-chill Ein Shemer, Dolgo, and Gala sit comfortably under the confirmed range. The high-chill varieties, McIntosh, Honeycrisp, Zestar!, Empire, Golden Delicious, Jonagold, and Liberty, all need about 700 hours or more and are unproven for the Las Vegas Valley; the trial did not confirm them, so treat them as a gamble here rather than a recommendation.
apple.chill_basis_beginner: The desert here gives a few hundred chill hours, enough for low and moderate chill apples. Choose the varieties a University of Nevada field trial confirmed for Las Vegas, such as Dorsett Golden, Anna, Pink Lady, Fuji, Mutsu, and Granny Smith. The highest-chill types like Honeycrisp, McIntosh, and Golden Delicious need more winter cold than the valley reliably gives, so they are not a safe bet here.

apricot.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list here, including the higher chill Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich. Bloom runs into March and April, later than the valley floor, which trims the late frost risk somewhat even though the growing season starts later.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The higher, cooler parts of the region get more winter chill, so every apricot variety here has a good chance, even higher chill kinds like Moorpark and Chinese (Mormon). Bloom comes a little later, which helps dodge frost.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in March and April usually clears the mid March last frost; an unusually late cold snap during bloom is the occasional risk to watch, more so at the higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 (the Las Vegas Valley floor) banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, enough to fruit apricot dependably with the right variety: Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, and Harglow all clear the band, while the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich sit at the ceiling and are the first to disappoint in a mild winter. Bloom in late February to March is early enough that a late cold snap is an occasional risk; the dry air otherwise keeps disease low.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Apricots fruit reliably in the Las Vegas Valley if you choose a low or moderate chill variety like Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, or Harglow. Bloom comes early, so watch for a late frost, but the dry air means disease is rarely the problem.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late valley frost; more years than not it clears, and the dry air otherwise keeps disease pressure low.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin and the Colorado River corner (zone 10) bank the least chill, roughly 150 to 450 hours, so only the lowest chill varieties, Katy and Blenheim, fruit dependably; Tilton, Moorpark, Harglow, and the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich need more cold than this warm corner reliably banks. Bloom is very early here, mid February into March; summer heat and sunburn on young bark are the bigger concern than frost.
10.suitability_note_beginner: It is warmest at Laughlin, with the least winter chill, so stick to Katy or Blenheim. Heat and sun, not frost, are the main challenge here.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limit at Laughlin; low winter chill for the higher chill varieties, and intense summer heat, are the real constraints.

apricot.region_notes_beginner: Apricots do well across the Las Vegas Valley region if you match the variety to your zone. Katy and Blenheim are the safest, lowest chill picks and will fruit everywhere in the region, including the warm Laughlin corner. Moorpark, Tilton, and Harglow need more winter cold and are better suited to the valley floor and the cooler zone 8 pockets. Plant a bare root or container tree while it is dormant, from December through February, and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.
apricot.region_notes_seasoned: Apricot fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region when the variety is matched to the zone's chill. Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, enough for Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, and Harglow, with the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich right at the edge. The cooler zone 8 pockets clear the whole list with margin, while the warm Laughlin corner (zone 10) reliably suits only the lowest chill picks, Katy and Blenheim. Bloom comes very early (mid February through March depending on zone), which puts the crop at some risk from a late frost; the dry desert air otherwise keeps disease pressure low, so heat and sunburn on young bark, not brown rot, are the summer concern. Plant bare root or container trees during the dormant season.
apricot.chill_basis_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours in zone 9, more in the cooler zone 8 pockets and less at Laughlin in zone 10. That covers a genuine spread of apricot chill needs: Katy (about 350 hours), Blenheim (450), Tilton and Harglow (600 to 650), and Moorpark (650) all fit zone 9 with room to spare, while Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich sit right at the 700 hour ceiling, workable most years but the first to miss in a warm winter. Zone 8's wider band clears the whole list comfortably. At Laughlin (zone 10), only the lowest chill picks, Katy and Blenheim, are a safe bet; the 600 hour and up varieties need more cold than that warm corner reliably delivers.
apricot.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters here give apricots a real range of chill, more in the cooler zone 8 areas, less at warm Laughlin. Low chill varieties like Katy and Blenheim are the safest choice everywhere; the higher chill kinds such as Moorpark, Tilton, and Harglow do well in zone 9 and zone 8 but are a gamble at Laughlin.

cherry-sour.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, enough to give North Star, Meteor, and English Morello a genuine chance since all three need 700 to 800 hours; Montmorency and Balaton, at about 1000 hours, still fall short. This is the best sour cherry site the region offers, though still marginal without a local trial to confirm it.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The higher, cooler parts of the region give sour cherry its best shot here. Choose North Star, Meteor, or English Morello; skip Montmorency and Balaton, they need more cold than even this cooler zone provides.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in March to April usually clears the last frost; chill, not frost, is the limiting factor for this crop.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, which just touches the 700 hour floor of the lowest chill sour cherries, North Star and English Morello. That is a thin, top of the band fit: a slightly below average winter will fall short, and Meteor (800), Montmorency, and Balaton (1000) need more cold than this zone delivers in any year. Treat sour cherry as an experiment here, not a sure crop.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Sour cherry is a stretch on the valley floor. Only the lowest chill varieties, North Star and English Morello, have any real chance, and even they need a colder than average winter.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March usually clears frost; the binding limit here is winter chill, not a late freeze.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks only about 150 to 450 chill hours, well short of even the lowest chill sour cherry variety's 700 hour need. This is the weakest sour cherry site in the region; expect little to no reliable fruiting.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is too warm in winter for sour cherry. None of the recommended varieties get enough cold there.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not the issue at Laughlin; insufficient winter chill is what limits sour cherry here.

cherry-sour.region_notes_beginner: Sour cherry is a difficult crop for the Las Vegas Valley region. Even the lowest chill varieties, North Star, Meteor, and English Morello, need more winter cold than the valley floor and Laughlin reliably give, and the classic Montmorency and Balaton need more still. The cooler zone 8 pockets are the best bet, but even there it is a marginal crop, not a sure thing. If you want a cherry here, expect to experiment and accept some years without fruit.
cherry-sour.region_notes_seasoned: Sour cherry is marginal across the Las Vegas Valley region: its lowest chill named varieties, North Star and English Morello, need about 700 hours, right at or above what any Nevada zone reliably banks, and the classic Montmorency and Balaton (about 1000 hours) are essentially out of reach everywhere here. The cooler zone 8 pockets (roughly 500 to 900 hours) give North Star, Meteor, and English Morello their best, though still unproven, chance; the valley floor and Laughlin fall short even of those. Bloom is early and the dry air keeps disease low, but chill, not frost or disease, is what limits this crop in the desert.
cherry-sour.chill_basis_seasoned: Sour cherry is a genuinely high chill crop: North Star and English Morello need about 700 hours, Meteor about 800, and the classic Montmorency and Balaton about 1000, all well above what most of the Las Vegas Valley banks. Zone 8's cooler pockets (roughly 500 to 900 hours) reach far enough to give North Star, Meteor, and English Morello a real, if unproven, chance; Montmorency and Balaton need more cold than even zone 8 reliably delivers. Zone 9 (roughly 300 to 700 hours) sits North Star and English Morello right at the very top edge, workable only in an unusually cold winter, and Laughlin (zone 10, 150 to 450 hours) falls well short of every variety on the list.
cherry-sour.chill_basis_beginner: Sour cherries need a lot of winter cold, more than most of this desert region reliably provides. The cooler zone 8 pockets come closest, giving lower chill picks like North Star, Meteor, and English Morello a shot, though still not a sure thing. The valley floor and Laughlin are too warm in winter for a dependable sour cherry crop.

cherry-sweet.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including Bing (800 hours) and the 700 hour self-fertile standards, with real margin. This is the strongest sweet cherry site in the region.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region grow the widest range of sweet cherries, including Bing, with plenty of winter cold to spare.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in March to April usually clears the last frost; a late cold snap at the higher elevations is the occasional risk.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 (the Las Vegas Valley floor) banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours. The low chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal (about 250 hours, plant both together) is a dependable fit here. The 700 hour self-fertile standards, Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian, sit right at the ceiling and crop most years but are the first to disappoint in a mild winter; Bing (800 hours) needs more cold than this zone reliably delivers.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, the safest sweet cherry choice is the Royal Lee and Minnie Royal pair, planted together. The familiar varieties like Stella and Lapins usually do fine too, but a warm winter can shortchange them.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late frost; the dry air keeps disease pressure low regardless.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks only about 150 to 450 chill hours. Only the low chill pair, Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, planted together, reliably clears that band; the 700 to 800 hour standards need more cold than this warm corner provides.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At warm Laughlin, plant Royal Lee and Minnie Royal together; the other sweet cherry varieties need more winter cold than this spot gets.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue at Laughlin; the limiting factor for the higher chill varieties is winter chill, not cold snaps.

cherry-sweet.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry can fruit across the Las Vegas Valley region if you pick the right variety for your area. Royal Lee and Minnie Royal are a low chill pair bred for mild winters; plant them together (they need each other to pollinate) and they will fruit reliably everywhere, including Laughlin. On the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 pockets, the familiar self-fertile varieties like Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian are also a good bet. Bing needs the most winter cold and a separate pollinizer tree, so it is best kept to the cooler zone 8 areas.
cherry-sweet.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region with the right variety choice. The low chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal (about 250 hours each, and mutually required for pollination since neither is self-fertile) clears every zone here, including Laughlin, and is the dependable choice region-wide. The self-fertile 700 hour standards, Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian, sit right at zone 9's chill ceiling (workable most years) and fit zone 8's wider band comfortably. Bing, at 800 hours and needing a separate pollinizer, is best reserved for zone 8. Bloom is early and the dry desert air keeps brown rot and bacterial canker pressure low; a late frost on the open bloom is the more relevant risk.
cherry-sweet.chill_basis_seasoned: Sweet cherry splits into two very different chill tiers here. Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, a purpose-bred low chill pair that must be planted together for pollination, need only about 250 hours and clear every Nevada zone with room to spare, including Laughlin. The self-fertile standards, Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian, need about 700 hours, which sits right at zone 9's ceiling (workable in most years) and comfortably inside zone 8's wider band; Bing, at 800 hours and not self-fertile on top of that, is better reserved for zone 8. Laughlin (zone 10) is a Royal Lee and Minnie Royal site only.
cherry-sweet.chill_basis_beginner: Sweet cherry works two ways in this desert region. Royal Lee and Minnie Royal are a low chill pair bred for mild winters like this one; plant them together and they fruit reliably everywhere, even at warm Laughlin. The familiar market varieties like Stella, Lapins, and Rainier need more winter cold and do best on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 areas; Bing needs the most cold and a pollinizer besides, so it is a zone 8 pick.

nectarine.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including the higher chill Roseprincess, Redgold, Hardired, and Mericrest. This is the widest variety choice in the region.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region can grow any of the recommended nectarines, including the higher chill kinds.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late frost after bloom in March to April is the main risk here, more so at the higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, clearing Arctic Star, Fantasia, Flavortop, and Independence, with the 700 hour Independence right at the ceiling. Roseprincess, Redgold, Hardired, and Mericrest need more chill than this zone reliably banks. Bloom is very early, late February into March, so a late cold snap is the main risk, alongside summer sunburn.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, Arctic Star, Fantasia, Flavortop, and Independence are solid choices. Watch for a late frost right after the early bloom, and shade young bark from summer sun.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The very early bloom occasionally meets a late valley frost; more often the tree comes through fine and the summer heat and sun are the bigger concern.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks roughly 150 to 450 chill hours. Arctic Star (300 hours) is a dependable fit; Fantasia (500) sits just past the ceiling and is a lesser bet. The higher chill cultivars are not viable here. Intense summer heat and sunburn, not frost, are the dominant hazards at this warmest zone.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At Laughlin, Arctic Star is the reliable choice. The heat here is intense, so shade young bark and expect some sunburn on exposed fruit.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a problem at Laughlin; the summer heat and sun are the real challenge.

nectarine.region_notes_beginner: Nectarine fruits well across the Las Vegas Valley region; low chill desert types like Arctic Star are a Southwest staple and grow everywhere here, including Laughlin. Fantasia, Flavortop, and Independence do well on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 pockets. The dry air keeps disease low, so the things to watch for are a late spring frost on the early bloom and sunburn on the fruit and young bark during the hot summer.
nectarine.region_notes_seasoned: Nectarine fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region, re-affirming the classic desert Southwest pairing of low chill stone fruit and dry heat. Zone 9's band clears Arctic Star, Fantasia, Flavortop, and Independence; the higher chill Roseprincess, Redgold, Hardired, and Mericrest need zone 8's cooler, higher pockets. Laughlin (zone 10) is an Arctic Star site. The dry desert air keeps brown rot low, unlike humid growing regions where it is the dominant risk; here the practical hazards are a late frost catching the very early bloom and sunburn on exposed fruit and young bark through the summer.
nectarine.chill_basis_seasoned: Nectarine is a genuine desert Southwest crop, and the chill numbers back that up here. Zone 9's roughly 300 to 700 hours covers Arctic Star (300), Fantasia (500), Flavortop (650), and Independence (700) comfortably to the ceiling; the higher chill Roseprincess, Redgold (750), Hardired (800), and Mericrest (850) need zone 8's wider 500 to 900 hour band. Laughlin (zone 10, 150 to 450 hours) suits Arctic Star reliably, with Fantasia at the edge. Unlike humid growing regions, the binding risk here is not brown rot; it is a late frost on the very early bloom and summer sunburn on exposed fruit and bark.
nectarine.chill_basis_beginner: This is real nectarine country: the desert's dry winters and hot summers suit it well. Arctic Star, the lowest chill variety, fruits everywhere in the region, even at Laughlin. Fantasia and Flavortop do well on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 areas; the higher chill kinds like Hardired and Mericrest need the extra cold of zone 8.

peach.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing Florida King and the 800 to 850 hour standards, Redhaven, Belle of Georgia, Elberta, Cresthaven, and J.H. Hale, with real margin. Contender and Reliance (1000 hours and up) still need more cold than even this zone banks.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region grow the widest range of peaches, including the classic Redhaven and Elberta types.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late frost after the March to April bloom is the main risk here, more so at higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours. Florida King (400 hours) is a dependable fit; the 800 hour standards like Redhaven and Elberta need more chill than this zone reliably banks. Bloom is very early, so a late cold snap is the main risk, alongside summer sunburn on fruit and bark.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, Florida King is the reliable peach. The classic varieties like Redhaven need more winter cold than the valley floor consistently provides.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The early bloom occasionally meets a late valley frost; the desert's dry air otherwise keeps disease low.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks roughly 150 to 450 chill hours, enough for Florida King (400 hours) alone; the 800 hour and up standards are not viable this warm. Intense summer heat and sunburn, not frost, are the dominant hazards at this warmest zone.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At Laughlin, Florida King is the peach to plant. Expect intense summer heat; shade young bark and watch for sunburn on the fruit.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a problem at Laughlin; summer heat and sun are the real challenge.

peach.region_notes_beginner: Peach grows well across the Las Vegas Valley region; low chill desert peaches like Florida King are a Southwest staple and fruit everywhere here, including Laughlin. The familiar Redhaven, Elberta, and similar varieties do best in the cooler zone 8 pockets. The dry air keeps disease low, so watch instead for a late spring frost on the early bloom and sunburn on fruit and young bark through the hot summer.
peach.region_notes_seasoned: Peach fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region, the same dry heat and low chill pairing that makes the desert Southwest classic peach country. Florida King (400 hours) is the region-wide anchor, clearing every zone including Laughlin. The 800 to 850 hour standards, Redhaven, Belle of Georgia, Elberta, Cresthaven, and J.H. Hale, need zone 8's cooler, higher pockets; the high chill Contender and Reliance (1000 hours and up) do not fit anywhere in this region. Unlike humid growing regions, brown rot is not the binding constraint here; a late frost on the very early bloom and summer sunburn are the practical hazards.
peach.chill_basis_seasoned: Peach is the classic low chill desert Southwest fruit, and Las Vegas Valley chill supports it. Florida King (400 hours) clears zone 9, zone 8, and even Laughlin's 150 to 450 hour band; it is the dependable region-wide anchor. The familiar 800 to 850 hour standards, Redhaven, Belle of Georgia, Elberta, Cresthaven, and J.H. Hale, need zone 8's wider 500 to 900 hour band and are unproven at zone 9's 700 hour ceiling. Contender and Reliance, at 1000 to 1050 hours, need more winter cold than any Nevada zone reliably banks and are not a fit here. As in the rest of the arid Southwest, the practical risks are a late frost on the early bloom and summer sunburn, not the brown rot that limits peach in humid regions.
peach.chill_basis_beginner: Peach is a natural fit for this desert region, the same low chill desert peach tradition found across the Southwest. Florida King, the lowest chill variety, fruits everywhere here, even at Laughlin. The classic varieties like Redhaven and Elberta need more winter cold and do best in the cooler zone 8 pockets. Contender and Reliance need more cold than this region reliably gets, so they are not a good choice here.

plum.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including the European prune plums Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson. This is the widest plum variety choice in the region.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region can grow any of the recommended plums, including the European prune types.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late frost after the March to April bloom is an occasional risk here; steady irrigation through summer matters more.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, clearing the Japanese plums Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank comfortably, with Green Gage (700 hours) right at the ceiling. Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson need more chill than this zone reliably banks.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, plant a Japanese plum like Methley, Santa Rosa, or Burbank for a reliable crop. Green Gage usually works too, but the European prune plums need more winter cold than the valley floor consistently gives.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late frost; the dry air otherwise keeps disease low, and regular deep watering matters more than either.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks roughly 150 to 450 chill hours, enough for the Japanese plums Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank; Green Gage and the European prune plums need more cold than this warm corner provides.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At Laughlin, stick to a Japanese plum like Methley, Santa Rosa, or Burbank. The European types need more winter cold than this spot gets.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a problem at Laughlin; intense summer heat and the need for steady water are the bigger considerations.

plum.region_notes_beginner: Plum grows well across the Las Vegas Valley region. The Japanese plums, Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank, are a classic low chill desert Southwest choice and fruit everywhere here, including Laughlin. Green Gage does well on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 areas. The European prune plums, Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson, need more winter cold and are best kept to the cooler zone 8 pockets. Deep, regular watering through the hot summer is essential.
plum.region_notes_seasoned: Plum fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region, splitting cleanly between the low chill Japanese types and the higher chill European prune plums. Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank (250 to 400 hours) are the dependable, desert-adapted anchor, clearing every zone including Laughlin. Green Gage (700 hours) fits zone 9 at the edge and zone 8 comfortably. Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson (800 to 900 hours) need zone 8's cooler, higher pockets. The dry air keeps disease low; irrigation, not frost or chill, is the defining requirement through the hot growing season.
plum.chill_basis_seasoned: Plum splits cleanly along species lines here. The low chill Japanese plums, Methley (250 hours), Santa Rosa, and Burbank (400 each), are a classic desert Southwest fit and clear every Nevada zone, including Laughlin. Green Gage, a European dessert plum at 700 hours, sits right at zone 9's ceiling and fits zone 8 comfortably. The high chill European prune plums, Stanley and Italian Prune (800 hours) and Damson (900), need zone 8's wider 500 to 900 hour band and are not a fit at zone 9 or Laughlin.
plum.chill_basis_beginner: Plum works well here if you pick the right type. The Japanese plums, Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank, are low chill desert classics that fruit everywhere in the region, even at Laughlin. The European prune plums like Stanley and Damson need more winter cold and are better suited to the cooler zone 8 pockets.

pear-asian.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including Olympic and Seuri with real margin.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region grow every recommended Asian pear variety without difficulty.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late frost after the March to April bloom is an occasional risk, more so at higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, clearing nearly the whole Asian pear list, Shinseiki, Ya Li, Tsu Li, 20th Century, Kosui, Hosui, Chojuro, Shinko, and Niitaka, with only Olympic and Seuri (500 hours) at the edge. Bloom in late February to March keeps a late frost as an occasional risk; the dry air keeps fire blight well controlled.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, almost every recommended Asian pear variety fruits well. Olympic and Seuri are a slightly tighter fit, but everything else is a safe bet.
